title: 15-Year Mortgage for Rental Property: Cash Flow Math
metaDescription: Is a 15-year mortgage for a rental property worth the higher payment? Compare cash flow, interest savings, equity pacing, and break-even rent.
h1: 15-Year Mortgage for Rental Property: Cash Flow and Math
cardBlurb: Modeled rental cash flow, interest savings, and break-even rent comparing a 15-year mortgage to a 30-year loan on an investment purchase.
introText:
A 15-year mortgage for a rental property makes financial sense only when monthly rent clears the higher loan payment. It must leave enough room for operating expenses. 

On a modeled $300,000 loan, the shorter loan term raises the monthly principal and interest payment by $582.31, which lifts your break-even rental income from $3,221.89 to $3,834.84 every month. At a hypothetical rent of $3,300 each month, a 30-year loan generates positive net cash flow of $74.21. The 15-year loan creates a monthly deficit of $508.10. Landlords must evaluate whether accelerated principal paydown balances out thinner monthly margins on rental property investments.

sections.heading: What a 15-Year Loan Does to Rental Cash Flow
sections.body:
A 15-year mortgage for rental property purchases increases your mandatory monthly debt payment while accelerating equity accumulation. In our internal modeling, we compared a 15-year and a 30-year loan on the same $300,000 rental purchase loan to see how much rent each needs. We used the [Freddie Mac](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms) averages for the week of October 22, 2026. Combined with our assumed $1,000 a month in other costs and 5% vacancy, we mapped payment schedules and interest totals. You can test your own figures in our [rental cash flow calculator](/real-estate/cash-flow-calculator/) using the standard fixed-rate amortization formula.

| Measure | 30-Year Loan (7.32%, Freddie Mac owner-occupied average) | 15-Year Loan (6.68%) | Difference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Monthly Payment (Principal and Interest) | $2,060.79 | $2,643.10 | +$582.31 |
| Total Interest Over Full Term | $441,885.07 | $175,757.86 | -$266,127.21 |
| Remaining Balance After 5 Years | $283,339.36 | $230,907.00 | -$52,432.36 |
| Remaining Balance After 10 Years | $259,342.16 | $134,504.96 | -$124,837.20 |
| Break-Even Monthly Rent (5% Vacancy + $1,000 Costs) | $3,221.89 | $3,834.84 | +$612.95 |

On a modeled $300,000 loan, selecting a 15-year term forces you to absorb a monthly payment increase of $582.31. That cash requirement pushes the monthly rent needed to break even up by $612.95 once vacancy loss is included. In exchange for managing that higher baseline obligation, you build equity faster. After 10 years of payments, the 15-year loan balance drops to $134,504.96, while the 30-year loan balance remains elevated at $259,342.16. Lifetime interest drops from $441,885.07 down to $175,757.86, saving $266,127.21 over the life of the debt.

To see how this affects your complete investment performance over time, review your expected overall yield with our [rental property return on investment (ROI) calculator](/real-estate/roi-calculator/). The fundamental trade-off is clear: you forfeit current monthly spendable income to capture faster equity growth and save more than a quarter-million dollars in interest.

sections.heading: The Alternative: A 30-Year Loan Paid Like a 15-Year Loan
sections.body:
You can replicate much of the interest savings of a 15-year term by sending extra principal payments on a conventional 30-year note. If you borrow $300,000 at a 30-year rate of 7.32% and voluntarily remit the 15-year payment amount of $2,643.10 each month, the loan amortizes in about 193.8 months, or roughly 16.15 years. You retire the debt nearly on the 15-year schedule while preserving payment flexibility. You can review the exact payoff timeline by running your numbers through our [mortgage payoff calculator](/mortgage/payoff-calculator/).

Total interest paid using this prepay strategy reaches $212,347.96. That total is $36,590.10 higher than the $175,757.86 interest on the actual 15-year note, but it cuts $229,537.11 off the standard 30-year interest cost of $441,885.07. That $36,590.10 reflects the model's lower 15-year rate (6.68% against 7.32%, both Freddie Mac owner-occupied averages). In our baseline scenario, the 15-year rate is 6.68%, which sits 64 basis points below the 30-year rate of 7.32%.

The structural benefit of the 30-year structure is that extra principal payments remain voluntary. Your contractual obligation stays locked at $2,060.79 a month. If a tenant moves out or costly maintenance arises, you can immediately drop your remittance back to the mandatory $2,060.79 floor. A true 15-year mortgage legally obligates you to pay $2,643.10 every month regardless of property occupancy.

Our perspective on this choice would change if investment property rate quotes eliminate the interest rate spread between the two terms. If a lender quotes the exact same interest rate on both terms, taking the 15-year loan forfeits payment flexibility without securing any rate discount. You can compare loan mechanisms in detail in our [15-year vs 30-year mortgage comparison](/compare/15-year-vs-30-year-mortgage/). Ask your lender whether the loan has a prepayment penalty.

sections.heading: How Much Rent You Need for a 15-Year Investment Property
sections.body:
Calculating your required rent begins with the break-even formula where net rent covers both debt service and operating costs. In our core model, we assume $1,000 in monthly expenses covering maintenance, management, insurance, and taxes, along with an ongoing 5% vacancy allowance. Because 5% of gross rent is lost to vacancy, the remaining 95% of gross rent must equal your monthly loan payment plus $1,000 of fixed costs. You can calculate your net rental figures directly with our [rental income calculator](/real-estate/rental-income-calculator/).

To see how rate variations influence required leasing rates, consider these hypothetical rate scenarios for a 15-year mortgage for rental property purchases on a $300,000 balance. The rate premiums shown below are hypothetical examples designed to show math sensitivity, not lender quotes:

| 15-Year Loan Scenario | Monthly Payment | Break-Even Rent (5% Vacancy + $1,000 Costs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Base Loan (6.68%, Freddie Mac owner-occupied average) | $2,643.10 | $3,834.84 |
| Hypothetical +0.50% Premium (7.18%) | $2,726.76 | $3,922.91 |
| Hypothetical +1.00% Premium (7.68%) | $2,811.81 | $4,012.43 |

At the base 6.68% rate, you need gross rent of $3,834.84 to break even. A hypothetical 0.50 percentage point rate increase to 7.18% lifts the debt payment to $2,726.76, pushing break-even rent to $3,922.91. A full 1.00 percentage point increase to 7.68% raises the loan obligation to $2,811.81 and requires $4,012.43 in monthly rent just to cover basic costs.

Take a hypothetical rent of $3,300 a month. After accounting for the 5% vacancy deduction ($165.00), you collect $3,135.00 in effective monthly income. Subtracting $1,000 in operational costs leaves $2,135.00 in net operating income before debt payments.

On the 30-year loan at $2,060.79 per month, your net cash flow equals +$74.21 each month ($2,135.00 minus $2,060.79). On the 15-year loan at $2,643.10 per month, your net cash flow drops to -$508.10 each month ($2,135.00 minus $2,643.10). An investor on the 15-year schedule must contribute $508.10 out of pocket each month to keep the property running. You must determine if your cash reserves can absorb a regular monthly deficit in exchange for rapid equity build.

sections.heading: Rate Inputs and Model Limits
sections.body:
The interest rates used in these models derive from the weekly averages published by [Freddie Mac](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms) in its Primary Mortgage Market Survey as of October 22, 2026. In that release, the national average for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.32%, while the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.68%. For historical context, one week earlier the 30-year averaged 7.40% and the 15-year was 6.71%. One year prior, the 30-year averaged 6.19% and the 15-year stood at 5.44%.

The Freddie Mac survey gathers rate information from lenders submitting conforming loan applications across the country. The survey measures purchase loans for owner-occupied, single-family primary residences for borrowers with good or excellent credit. Because the survey reflects owner-occupied primary residences, it does not describe investment-property financing. Lenders may price investment properties differently, meaning your actual quote may differ. Fees and points are not published in the survey. You should contact lenders directly to get investment-property quotes for your specific transaction.

The calculations incorporate author assumptions of $1,000 a month in combined non-mortgage operating costs and a 5% vacancy rate. These expense levels are illustrative baseline assumptions rather than market data. 

Furthermore, this model excludes income taxes, federal depreciation deductions, closing costs, required liquid reserves, future rental rate increases, loan points, and mortgage insurance. It also omits the detailed qualification guidelines that lenders apply to investment borrowers. For deeper context on operational tax write-offs, consult our guide on [rental property tax deductions](/guides/rental-property-tax-deductions/).

sections.heading: Qualifying for a Shorter Term on an Investment Purchase
sections.body: The 15-year payment is higher ($2,643.10 against $2,060.79 on the modeled $300,000 loan). This raises the monthly obligation a lender weighs against income. Ask a licensed mortgage professional how a lender counts rent and your debts. Evaluate your borrowing power with our [home affordability calculator](/mortgage/home-affordability-calculator/).

sections.heading: Who This Loan Fits and Who Should Avoid It
sections.body:
A 15-year mortgage for rental property investments is not suitable for an investor operating with narrow profit margins. If a rental unit commands market rent close to the $3,222 baseline needed for a 30-year loan, taking a 15-year term forces a monthly operational deficit. Investors facing big near-term repairs should also avoid the shorter term. Repairs come out of the same cash the higher payment uses.

Similarly, buyers who want maximum monthly cash flow should pass on 15-year financing. In our $3,300 rent scenario, the 30-year note leaves positive cash flow. The 15-year note demands monthly out-of-pocket contributions. You can explore how distributions align with long-term goals in our analysis of whether you [can retire on rental income](/guides/can-i-retire-on-rental-income/), or compare direct property ownership with indirect trusts in our [real estate investment trust (REIT) vs rental property comparison](/compare/reit-vs-rental-property/).

Conversely, a 15-year loan fits a landlord whose property commands gross rent well above the $3,835 break-even threshold. It also suits landlords who prioritize faster equity accumulation and total interest reduction over monthly cash flow. In the model it saves $266,127 in financing costs.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
Based on our internal modeling using Freddie Mac owner-occupied averages, a 15-year term on a $300,000 loan saves approximately $266,127 in lifetime interest and reduces the principal balance to $134,505 after 10 years, compared to $259,342 on a 30-year loan. However, achieving those savings requires managing a mandatory monthly payment that is $582 higher. That pushes the break-even gross rent up by roughly $613 per month.

This structure fits an investor with strong rental margins and healthy reserves who targets rapid debt elimination. It does not fit an investor who needs monthly cash flow or who operates in a market where prevailing rents cannot absorb the higher debt service. Additionally, paying the 15-year payment amount on a flexible 30-year mortgage pays the balance off in roughly 16.2 years with $36,590 in additional interest. It also preserves the option to remit the lower payment during tenant turnover.

Your actual outcome will vary based on the specific investment property mortgage rates you are quoted, local operating expenses, and sustained occupancy. To evaluate debt terms for your situation, consult a licensed mortgage professional and request formal loan estimates from multiple lenders. Model your property numbers through our [rental cash flow calculator](/real-estate/cash-flow-calculator/) before committing to a 15-year mortgage for rental property financing.

faqs.question: What is the monthly payment on a $100,000 15-year loan?
faqs.answer: At a 6.68% interest rate, the monthly principal and interest payment on a $100,000 15-year loan is approximately $881.03. By comparison, a 30-year loan on $100,000 at a 7.32% interest rate requires about $686.93 per month. These figures reflect the Freddie Mac survey averages published on October 22, 2026 for owner-occupied purchases, meaning actual investment property quotes will vary.

faqs.question: Is it harder to qualify for a 15-year mortgage?
faqs.answer: The 15-year payment is higher ($2,643.10 against $2,060.79 on the modeled $300,000 loan), which raises the monthly obligation a lender weighs against income. Ask a licensed mortgage professional how a lender counts rent and your debts.

faqs.question: Is a 15-year mortgage good for an investment property?
faqs.answer: A 15-year mortgage works well if your gross rent comfortably exceeds the higher break-even threshold and you prioritize debt elimination over current cash flow. In our model, it saves $266,127 in interest. If your rental margins are thin or you experience tenant turnover, the higher monthly obligation can create cash flow strain.

faqs.question: How fast does a 15-year loan build equity compared with a 30-year?
faqs.answer: A 15-year loan builds equity faster than a 30-year loan. On a $300,000 loan, the remaining balance after 5 years is $230,907.00 for the 15-year term versus $283,339.36 for the 30-year term. After 10 years, the 15-year balance falls to $134,504.96, while the 30-year balance sits at $259,342.16.

faqs.question: Can I pay a 30-year mortgage off in 15 years?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can pay off a 30-year loan early by making higher monthly payments. Paying the 15-year payment of $2,643.10 on a 30-year loan at 7.32% (Freddie Mac owner-occupied average) pays off the debt in about 193.8 months, or roughly 16.15 years. You pay about $36,590.10 more in total interest than a true 15-year loan, but you retain the option to pay the lower $2,060.79 minimum payment if needed.

faqs.question: What are rates for investment-property loans?
faqs.answer: Specific investment-property rates are not published in the Freddie Mac survey, which only tracks owner-occupied single-family residential purchases. Lenders may price investment loans with different rates and fees. You should contact lenders directly to receive quotes for investment-property financing.
